sulfur of nature is hardened, after a small amount of heat, which pertains to silver, provided it is also informed with the shape of silver, whereby gold can likewise be made just as from other metals, unless it is deprived of its own heat, or the natural operation is not taken away from it. But if the power of a greater natural heat should approach that quicksilver before it has been formed into its final state, namely into the form of silver, so that it is reduced into the pure and red sulfur of nature, then gold is made from it more quickly than silver, and it remains in that state perpetually, as the end toward which nature tends by its labor.

Quicksilver, which we have just mentioned, is the mother of all metals because of its coldness and humidity; and if it be pure and separated from all superfluity, then no further thickness can be mixed with it, so that it might be driven back again into some imperfect metal. For nature does not work backward, nor is it a matter that looks toward any impure form, such as imperfect metals are. But sulfur is the father of all metals because of its heat and dryness. According to this difference, let it be observed that quicksilver is described in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER II.

There is therefore in all metals a true <term>Mercury</term> <gloss>quicksilver</gloss> and a right <term>sulfur</term>, equally in imperfect as well as in perfect metals; only it has been made contaminated and impure in the imperfect metals, which are those alone that lack perfect maturation. And for these same reasons they can be reduced to gold and silver, that is, so that the impurity with which they had been defiled may be separated from the golden or silver nature that is within them, and the form of gold or silver may be introduced into them. For they were snatched away from nature for this reason: because they were removed and dug out from the natural passages, mines, and veins of the earth; therefore they can no longer have any operation within themselves, as if they were still hiding under the earth. Nevertheless, as much as is within them, they desire to be perfected.

<summary>This page defines mercury as the mother and sulfur as the father of all metals. It argues that even base metals contain the essence of gold and silver and can be refined into them if their impurities are removed, despite being prematurely extracted from the earth.</summary>
